Inaugurate

in-AW-gyuh-rayt -- from Latin inaugurare ('to consecrate by reading omens'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To inaugurate to formally begin or introduce something, typically with a ceremony.

The university will inaugurate its new research wing next month with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Worked Example

The town chose to inaugurate its brand-new fire station with a parade, free hot dogs, and a speech from the mayor.

Notice the ceremony -- a parade, food, a speech. Inaugurate isn't just 'starting' something quietly; it's marking a formal beginning with deliberate fanfare.

launch: to start something new and set it in motion

Antonyms

conclude: to bring something to its end

terminate

How Strong Is It? — launch → inaugurate → commission

launch vs. inaugurate

launch vs. inaugurate: Launch is weaker than inaugurate: a company can launch an app with one quiet online announcement, while inaugurating something carries the full weight of a formal opening ceremony.

commission vs. inaugurate

commission vs. inaugurate: Commission goes further than inaugurate: inaugurating ceremonially begins something, while commissioning a warship formally invests it with active duty, honor guard, christening and all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — -augur-

root — -augur-: to foretell, consecrate by omens (Latin (augur))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin inaugurare meant to consecrate an official after reading favorable omens, from in- ('into') plus augur ('omen-reader'), with the verb suffix -ate. To inaugurate something still means giving it a formal, ceremonial beginning.

Use the root in a new word: augury

Use the root in a new word: augury: The unusually calm weather on launch day felt like a good augury for the mission's success.

Root Check

Word Choice

Inaugurate is about the formal, ceremonial launch of something -- a building, a policy, an official's term. Compare Nascent, which describes something naturally just beginning to grow with no ceremony involved, and Inchoate, which is about something raw and unformed, not about how it was launched.
